segments.text: [style: brisk, clear, architectural voice; steady studio cadence] Book Three, Proposition Twenty-Seven. In equal circles, angles standing on equal arcs are equal to one another, whether they stand at the centers or at the arcs. Let A B C and D E F be equal circles, and on equal arcs B C and E F let angles B G C and E H F stand at the centers G and H, and angles B A C and E D F stand at the arcs. We must prove that angle B G C equals E H F, and angle B A C equals E D F.

segments.text: [style: methodical, precise constructive cadence] For if angle B G C is unequal to angle E H F, one of them is greater. Let B G C be greater, and on segment B G at G, construct angle B G K equal to angle E H F by One Twenty-Three.

segments.text: [style: luminous, deductive geometric clarity] Because equal central angles stand on equal arcs by Three Twenty-Six, arc B K equals arc E F. But arc E F was given equal to arc B C; therefore arc B K equals arc B C, the less to the greater, which is impossible. Thus central angle B G C is not unequal to E H F, so B G C equals E H F. And by Three Twenty, the inscribed angle B A C is half of central angle B G C, and angle E D F is half of E H F. Therefore angle B A C also equals angle E D F, as was required to prove.

segments.text: [style: reflective, scholarly, architectural synthesis] Proposition Twenty-Seven is the exact converse of Three Twenty-Six. Rather than repeating the chord-and-segment construction in reverse, Euclid deploys a crisp indirect proof: copying the central angle immediately forces a proper sub-arc to equal the whole arc, violating Common Notion Five, while Three Twenty transfers equality from the center to the circumference in a single stroke. In the GEOMETOR G-Index, node G one-thirty-four unites eight direct rules across sixty ancestor nodes, establishing the bidirectional equivalence between arc length and angular measure.
